title: Fatigue and Recovery after Single-Stage versus Multistage Ultramarathon Running
authors: Besson T, Rossi J, Le Roux Mallouf T, Marechal M, Doutreleau S, Verges S, Millet GY
population: 31 ultramarathon runners on the same course: 17 ran 169 km in one stage, 14 ran about 40 km/day over 4 days
findings: Neuromuscular function (knee extensors and plantar flexors, voluntary and nerve-stimulated) tested before, after, and 2, 5 and 10 days after the races.
Reduction of knee-extensor voluntary activation (central fatigue) was greater after the single-stage race than the multistage race directly after the finish (-23% vs -7%, P < 0.01).
Reductions in evoked mechanical responses on relaxed knee-extensor and plantar-flexor muscle (peripheral fatigue) took longer to recover in the multistage group than in the single-stage group.

Authors conclude that running prolonged exercise over several days, each separated by rest, elicits more prolonged contractile impairment than a single-stage ultramarathon, which is associated with greater central fatigue.
limitations: Non-randomised comparison of two self-selected groups; the abstract gives no numeric recovery values for D+2, D+5 and D+10, so it cannot date full recovery after the single-stage race; full text not read.
implications: Supports that a single 100-mile effort leaves a mainly central deficit that is large immediately and has faster peripheral recovery than multi-day stacked running; a hold followed by a graded return is consistent with this, but the paper gives no day count.

Do not use this paper to set specific day thresholds; use it as supporting context that running load in the days after a race (not just race distance) may prolong contractile impairment, so extra running in the days after a race should be kept small. This is an extrapolation, since the multistage design is not post-race running.

verification.notes: Crossref and PubMed esummary give a different author list (Besson, Rossi, Le Roux Mallouf, Marechal, Doutreleau, Verges, Millet); corrected. Abstract re-read unstripped from Europe PMC (PMID 32079919): -23% vs -7% P < 0.01, peripheral recovery slower in multistage, conclusion all present. Added caveat that the implication is an extrapolation.
